Under the heading "3.2 Phonology" the image reads exactly: "In Mam, short unstressed vowels are usualy dropped before a stressed vowel (cf. England 1983, 43-4). Sipakapense has adopted this process of dropping vowels before stress (which generally falls on the last syllable of a word). Thus, many root vowels drop or surface depending on morphology:" -- verbatim, including the original's "usualy". The examples in (9) on the same page carry acute accents on the final syllable (iʃiím "corn", w+ʃím "my corn", ʃ+ø+in+b'án "I did it", t…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the last syllable of the word, regardless of syllable weight (vowel length does not attract stress). Feet are quantity-insensitive iambs built right-to-left, so in the 2002 transcription secondary stress lands on every second syllable counting leftward from the final one. Short vowels in the syllable before the stressed one are deleted, which is why Sipakapense words carry long consonant clusters.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Barrett 2002, example (14), marks secondary stress (grave accent) on alternating syllables leftward from the final primary stress (kùuwìts'ulí, kàtktsulí, katìntsulí), i.e. right-to-left iambic footing, and calls the system quantity-insensitive. Bennett 2016 (sec. 6.1.1) explicitly lists Barrett 1999, 2002 among impressionistic secondary-stress reports that 'should be treated with caution'.
new_statements.exceptions: Barrett 1996 hedges with 'generally'. Barrett 2002 (p. 7) says the iambic system arose by reanalysis of the K'ichee' system on roots with an even number of syllables. The ALMG Gramática normativa (2011) and Monografía (2007) mention 'certain non-standard words accented on the penultimate syllable' shared with Cunén K'iche' (Kunenteko), used only as historical evidence, without listing them.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the 1996 statement is made while describing pre-tonic vowel syncope inside words (root vowels drop or surface depending on morphology); the 2002 examples are inflected verb forms and bare nouns (atí 'man', iiáq 'woman'). Nothing said about phrase-level or citation-form effects. Bennett 2016 (sec. 6.1) notes final stress is the K'ichean norm and that phrase-final prominence can be confused with word stress in the family.
new_statements.identity_note: Barrett's data are from the single Sipakapense-speaking community of Sipacapa, San Marcos (Glottolog sipa1247, no sub-dialects listed); older sources call the language Sipacapa / Sipacapeño / 'Quiche of Sipacapa' (Hoiland & Sánchez 1980). No identity problem.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Campbell's only stress statement is a family-level aside inside the Uspantec discussion: the Quichean languages other than Uspantec 'normally stress the final syllable'; Uspantec alone has innovated a (roughly penultimate) stress rule. Sipacapa is treated in the book as a Quiché dialect (morphology, future morphemes, -b' suffix), so the general final-stress statement covers it only by inclusion; no Sipacapa-specific stress sentence was found.
new_statements.exceptions: Uspantec (not Sipakapense) is the exception among Quichean languages; within Uspantec, monomorphemic disyllabic forms 'must be stated as exceptions'
new_statements.identity_note: Campbell 1977 calls the language 'Sipacapa' and classifies it as a Quiché dialect group ('The final group in Quiché is Sipacapa'); the stress sentence quoted is about the Quichean languages as a whole versus Uspantec, not about Sipacapa in particular. Barrett 1996/2002 (already held by the project) describe Sipakapense proper, western highlands southwest of Huehuetenango.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's fixed: final syllable record (Barrett 1996: stress 'generally falls on the last syllable') and with the existing Campbell 1977 statement held by the project; Still not a Sipacapa-specific stress sentence and still no page number.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level statement: the Quichean languages other than Uspantec normally stress the final syllable (Uspantec alone innovated a different, tone-linked rule: stress on the penultimate mora). Campbell treats Sipacapa as a dialect group of Quiché ('The final group in Quiché is Sipacapa'), so the final-stress default covers it; the Sipacapa paragraph itself gives no stress rule but reports loss of the first (pretonic) vowel of CVCVC roots (winaq > wnaq, tulul > tlul, sanik > snik, kuma¢ > kma¢), the same pre-stress vowel dropping Barrett 1996 describes. Also: Chinautla Pokomam 'stress always falls on the final syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing on secondary stress in the recovered fragments
new_statements.exceptions: Uspantec: innovated stress rule, 'stress upon the penultimate mora of a word', interacting with tone; Las Pacayas (Uspantec dialect) 'forms may either be stressed according to this rule, or on the final syllable, regardless of length'. No Sipacapa-specific exception seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Campbell 1977 treats Sipacapa (Sipakapense, spoken in Sipacapa, San Marcos, Guatemala) as a dialect group within Quiché ('The final group in Quiché is Sipacapa'), grouped with Sacapulas on shared morphology; its stress remark is about the Quichean languages as a set (minus Uspantec), not a Sipacapa-specific measurement. The catalog record rests on Barrett's fieldwork on Sipakapense proper.
